summary: For ages 12–13, learners work both directions on paired continuous data: they interpret what a line shows (a straight line indicates a constant-rate/linear relationship, and one through the origin — as in this spring data — is additionally proportional) AND construct the representation — a headed data table with ratio-form SI units, a graph type chosen from the data structure, accurately plotted points on evenly-scaled labelled axes, a single line of best fit, and a gradient read from two points on that line with its compound unit. The load-bearing work is construction with feedback at each step; recognition and value-reading tasks test the skill but do not themselves have the learner construct a table and graph from scratch. A spring extension vs load dataset makes the gradient a meaningful physical quantity (extension per unit load, in cm/N; this is the inverse of the spring's stiffness, which is load ÷ extension in N/cm).
misconceptions: Joining data points dot-to-dot and calling it a line graph, instead of drawing a single best-fit line.
Believing the line of best fit must pass through every point or always through the origin.
Reading the gradient from raw data points rather than from two points on the drawn line.
Choosing a bar chart when both variables are continuous (so the trend/relationship is lost).
Omitting units from table headings and axis labels, or writing them inside every cell instead of in the heading.
Using a non-uniform, cramped or origin-forced scale that distorts or hides the pattern.
Quoting a gradient as a bare number with no unit, treating it as dimensionless.

activities.title: Graphing Studio: from raw data to a gradient
steps: Start from a real paired dataset, e.g. spring extension vs load (Load / N: 1, 2, 3; Extension / cm: 3, 6, 9).
Type table column headings; a heading of 'Load' (or 'Mass') alone is flagged until you add the unit as a ratio, e.g. 'Load / N' or 'Mass / g', at which point the column is accepted.

Choose a graph type for the data: if you pick a bar chart for two continuous measures, the x-axis stays in discrete blocks and the trend cannot appear, prompting you to switch to a line/scatter graph so the axis becomes continuous.

Set the axis scales; a cramped scale (e.g. an axis running to 100 when the extensions only reach 9 cm) lights a 'wasted grid' meter and the points huddle in one corner, so you re-space in equal steps until the data fills at least about half the available grid using a sensible interval (1, 2, 5, 10).

Drag a single straight line through the point cloud; a live residual indicator shows points pulling above and below until the pulls balance, and the line deliberately does NOT have to pass through every point (nor be forced through the origin).

Interpret the line itself: a straight line shows a constant-rate (linear) relationship between extension and load, and because this data passes through the origin it is additionally proportional; the steepness tells you how much extension you get per unit load.

Click two well-separated points that lie ON the line (not raw data dots); the studio marks the rise and run, computes rise ÷ run, and asks you to write the gradient with its compound unit (e.g. cm/N, or mm/g for a mass-based setup).
State what the gradient means physically, e.g. extension per unit load (cm/N); a stiffer spring gives a smaller gradient, because stiffness is load ÷ extension (N/cm), the inverse of this gradient.
activities.insight: Each table/graph convention exists to make data readable and computable: the graph is not decoration but a machine for extracting a physical quantity, and the gradient is that quantity carried with its unit — while the shape of the line tells you about the relationship (a straight line means a constant rate, and through the origin it is proportional).

activities.title: Decide the display before you draw
steps: Given a described dataset, classify the independent variable as categoric (e.g. favourite colours) or continuous (e.g. load in newtons) BEFORE choosing any display.
Match: categoric IV → bar chart; continuous IV → line graph; two co-varying continuous measures → scatter graph.
Sort the two variables onto the correct axes: independent variable on the x-axis, dependent variable on the y-axis.
Explain for each case why the chosen display reveals (or a wrong one hides) the pattern.
activities.insight: Graph choice is a reasoned decision driven by the data structure, not a drawing habit; the right display preserves the relationship you want to read.

activities.title: Test your graphing: targeted question set
steps: Pick the correct graph type for a described dataset, including a distractor case where a bar chart is tempting but wrong because both variables are continuous.
Complete a table heading by supplying the correct SI unit in ratio form.
Sort given variables onto x- vs y-axis (IV vs DV).
Read a value off a plotted line of best fit using a slider/marker.
Sketch a line of best fit through a plotted point cloud.
Calculate a two-point gradient, reading points from the LINE not the raw data, and supply the compound unit.
activities.insight: Confirm that each convention — unit in heading, correct graph type, axis assignment, reading off the line, gradient with units — can be applied independently and under the classic error conditions.

activities.title: Good-vs-bad graph: annotated exemplar reference
steps: Study a correctly built table-and-graph with tap-to-reveal callouts: 'this heading shows the unit as a ratio', 'best-fit line balances points above and below', 'gradient = rise/run read from two points on the line'.
Compare it side by side with a flawed version (missing units, cramped/uneven scale, dot-to-dot join, gradient from a single raw point) and name each fault.
Use the exemplar as a reference while constructing your own graph.
activities.insight: A worked exemplar makes the conventions and their rationale explicit and provides a reference standard for self-checking.

checkQuestion: Here is a line graph of a spring's extension against load, with a straight best-fit line through the points. First, tell me what the line is telling us — what does its straightness and its steepness (gradient) mean about the spring? Then, from this results table (Load / N: 1, 2, 3; Extension / cm: 3, 6, 9) set up the table properly with headings and units, choose and start the right graph, and work out the gradient of the line — telling me what the gradient represents.
checkAnswer: Interpretation: the straight line means extension is proportional to load (a constant relationship); the gradient (steepness) is how much extension you get per newton — here 3 cm/N — the spring's stiffness. Translation: the child writes headings with quantity AND unit (Load / N, Extension / cm), chooses a line graph (continuous numerical data), plots with labelled, evenly-scaled axes, draws the best-fit line, and calculates gradient = change in extension ÷ change in load = 9 ÷ 3 = 3 cm/N, stating what it means.
